questions.question_text:
A tyre passes a pressure check $91\%$ of the time.
Let $X=1$ if the tyre **fails** the check.
Find $P(X=1)$.

options.why: Took passing the check as the success, but the question defines a failed check as the success.
Subtraction slip: wrote $1-0.91$ as $0.19$ instead of $0.09$.
Left the answer as a percentage instead of writing it as a probability.

questions.solution_text:
Success: the tyre fails the check.
$P(X=1)=1-0.91$
$=0.09$

options.why: Gave the probability of success rather than the probability of failure.
Borrowed incorrectly when subtracting, giving $1-0.42=0.68$.
Doubled $p$ instead of subtracting it from $1$.

questions.question_text:
One spin of a spinner lands on blue with probability $\frac{2}{7}$.
Let $X=1$ if the spin lands on blue.
Which table gives the distribution of $X$?

options.why: Swapped the probabilities, placing the success probability against $x=0$.
Used $1$ and $2$ as the values of $X$ instead of $0$ for failure and $1$ for success.
Swapped the probabilities and also used $1$ and $2$ as the values of $X$.

questions.question_text: In which of these is $X$ a Bernoulli random variable?

options.text: One randomly chosen email is checked, and $X=1$ if it is spam.
Twelve emails are checked, and $X$ is the number of them that are spam.
options.why: Counts successes over twelve trials, while a Bernoulli variable comes from exactly one trial.

options.text: One email is checked, and $X$ records whether it is spam, promotional or personal.
options.why: Three outcomes are recorded, but a Bernoulli trial must have exactly two.

options.text: Emails are checked until the first spam email appears, and $X$ is the number checked.
options.why: More than one trial can occur and $X$ takes many values, not just $0$ and $1$.

questions.solution_text:
A Bernoulli random variable comes from exactly one trial with exactly two outcomes.
Checking one email and recording whether it is spam fits both conditions.
The correct model is: one randomly chosen email is checked, and $X=1$ if it is spam.

questions.question_text:
A single chess game is played and the result — win, draw or loss — is recorded.
Why is this not a Bernoulli trial?

options.text: Three outcomes are recorded, but a Bernoulli trial must have exactly two.
The three outcomes do not all have the same probability.
options.why: A Bernoulli trial does not require its outcomes to be equally likely; only $p$ matters.

options.text: Only one game is played, and a Bernoulli variable needs several trials.
options.why: Reverses the definition: a Bernoulli variable comes from exactly one trial.

options.text: The result is not a number, so no random variable can be defined.
options.why: Non-numerical outcomes can always be coded as $0$ and $1$; that is not the problem here.

questions.solution_text:
A Bernoulli trial has exactly two possible outcomes.
Recording win, draw or loss gives three, so the trial is not Bernoulli.

questions.question_text:
A machine makes bolts and $6\%$ of them are undersized.
One bolt is chosen at random and $X=1$ if the bolt is **not** undersized.
Find $P(X=0)$.

options.why: Gave $P(X=1)$, the probability the bolt is not undersized, instead of $P(X=0)$.
Read $6\%$ as $0.6$ instead of $0.06$.
Read $6\%$ as $0.6$ and then also gave the probability of the other outcome.

questions.solution_text:
Success: the bolt is not undersized.
$P(X=0)=0.06$
